overview: This file documents an October 1940–January 1941 inquiry by the American President Lines and former senator William Gibbs McAdoo about maintaining automobile service and gasoline supplies at the company’s Kobe office under Japan’s wartime rationing regulations. Initial company reports alleged that foreign firms could no longer operate cars and that automobiles might be placed under American consular jurisdiction, but the State Department rejected that interpretation and requested a report from Kobe. Consul Samuel Sokobin subsequently explained that the company officially received eight gallons monthly plus a special allowance of 78 gallons, supplied through a United States payment arrangement with the Standard-Vacuum Oil Company, although its ration tickets were awaiting revalidation following stricter regulations effective October 1. The consular report also corrected confusion concerning the company’s Yokohama employee and the supposed precedent involving the Singer Sewing Machine Company, concluding that the Kobe office had adequate gasoline for the time being and did not yet want consular intervention.

subfiles.title: McAdoo requests assistance for the American President Lines automobile in Kobe
subfiles.from: William Gibbs McAdoo, Chairman of the Board, American President Lines
subfiles.to: Breckinridge Long, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: McAdoo asks the State Department to help license an American President Lines company automobile in Kobe so that it can continue operating and obtain fuel.
subfiles.summary: McAdoo forwards a letter from an American President Lines vice president concerning restrictions on oil and gasoline for company automobiles in Japan. He asks whether the State Department can arrange licensing of the Kobe company car in the manner suggested by Arthur B. Poole, arguing that this would facilitate the firm’s operations.

subfiles.title: Poole reports restrictions on foreign-owned automobiles in Japan
subfiles.from: Arthur B. Poole, American President Lines
subfiles.about: Poole asks McAdoo to consult the State Department about placing the company’s Kobe automobile under consular jurisdiction.
subfiles.summary: Poole reports Knight Aulsbrook’s claim that foreign companies were no longer permitted to operate automobiles or purchase gasoline in Japan. He repeats an account that cars belonging to American concerns could be placed under American consular jurisdiction and that the Singer Sewing Machine Company had already done so in Kobe. Concerned that Gabrielson would be seriously hampered without the company car, Poole asks McAdoo to seek State Department assistance.

subfiles.title: Long rejects proposed consular licensing arrangement
subfiles.from: Breckinridge Long, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Long replies that the State Department knows of no way to place the company automobile under the jurisdiction of the American Consulate.
subfiles.summary: Long states that he knows of no arrangement by which the Kobe automobile could be brought under American consular jurisdiction. He considers the alleged precedent involving another American company to be based on a misunderstanding. Nevertheless, the Department is forwarding the correspondence to the American Consul at Kobe.

subfiles.title: Instruction to the American Ambassador in Tokyo concerning the Kobe automobile
subfiles.about: The Department transmits McAdoo’s request and its reply to the American Ambassador for information.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State forwards copies of McAdoo’s October 12 letter and enclosure and the Department’s October 19 reply. The material concerns possible assistance with licensing an automobile belonging to the Kobe office of American President Lines. The instruction records field distribution to Tokyo and Kobe.

subfiles.title: Instruction to the American Consul in Kobe requesting comment
subfiles.about: The Department sends the correspondence to Kobe for the consul’s information and comment.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State encloses McAdoo’s request, its accompanying letter, and the Department’s response. Unlike the parallel instruction to the ambassador, this communication expressly requests comment from the American Consul. Copies were distributed to Kobe and Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Consular despatch on gasoline supplies for the Kobe company automobile
subfiles.from: Samuel Sokobin, American Consul at Kobe
subfiles.about: Sokobin explains the Kobe office’s gasoline allocation, ration-ticket difficulties, and reasons for declining immediate consular intervention.
subfiles.summary: After consulting manager Ernest Matteson, Sokobin reports that the company did not yet consider consular intervention desirable. Although the normal official allocation was only eight gallons per month, Japanese authorities had arranged an additional 78 gallons monthly because of the company’s prominence and because payment to Standard-Vacuum was made in the United States without Japanese foreign exchange. Ration tickets covering roughly 650 gallons from an annual 936-gallon special quota had been submitted for revalidation after stricter regulations took effect on October 1, but Matteson possessed an accumulated reserve and expected the tickets to be returned. Sokobin also clarifies that Gabrielson worked in Yokohama, not Kobe, and that the Singer Sewing Machine Company maintained no Kobe office and had made no automobile request to the consulate.

subfiles.title: Long forwards the Kobe consular report to McAdoo
subfiles.from: Breckinridge Long, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Long sends McAdoo the American Consulate’s report on gasoline supplies for the Kobe automobile.
subfiles.summary: Long follows up on McAdoo’s October inquiry about obtaining gasoline for the American President Lines automobile. He encloses Consular Despatch No. 66 of December 3, 1940, thereby providing the company with the detailed findings from Kobe.

interest: The file offers a compact case study of how Japanese fuel controls affected an American commercial enterprise shortly before the Pacific War and how private firms attempted to enlist diplomatic assistance. Sokobin’s despatch is especially valuable for its quantitative account of gasoline quotas, accumulated reserves, ration-ticket revalidation, and a payment arrangement designed to avoid Japanese foreign-exchange expenditure. The sequence also preserves the correction of rumors as information moved from company representatives in Japan through San Francisco and Washington and back to the Kobe consulate, revealing both the practical limits of consular jurisdiction and the mechanics of State Department case handling.
